ACT 01 · WHY DECENTRALIZE
The internet started open, then centralized
WEB 1 · 1980s–2000s
Open protocols
TCP/IP, HTTP, email. Nobody owns them, and anyone can build on them without asking permission.
WEB 2 · 2000s–NOW
Closed platforms
A few companies hold the users, the data and the rules. They attract you first, then extract from you.
WEB 3 · THE BET
Open networks that hold value
Networks owned by their users, with rules enforced by code that everyone can read.
Chris Dixon (a16z): software networks, unlike phone or TV networks, can be re-architected, and blockchains are that re-architecture.
01 · WHY DECENTRALIZE
Reading: Chris Dixon, "Why Decentralization Matters" (2018)
Who sits in the middle?
Centralized
One hub. If it fails or says no, everyone stops.
Decentralized
A few hubs. Sturdier, but the hubs still hold the power.
Distributed
No hub at all. Every node can route around failure.
Paul Baran sketched these three shapes in 1964 while designing a network that survives losing nodes. Blockchains apply the third shape to money.
01 · WHY DECENTRALIZE
After Paul Baran, "On Distributed Communications" (RAND, 1964)
The hard problem: digital money can be copied
A digital coin is just data, and data can be copied. What stops Alice from paying the same coin twice?
Alice
owns coin #42
Bob
receives coin #42
Carol
also receives coin #42
same coin, twice
Who really got paid?
The old fix: a trusted middleman
A bank keeps the one true ledger and rejects the second payment. It works, but now the bank is the hub.
Bitcoin's fix: everyone keeps the ledger
Thousands of computers hold a copy and agree on the order of payments. The first spend wins; the second is rejected.
01 · WHY DECENTRALIZE
What removing the middleman buys, and costs
No permission needed
Anyone can run a node, send a payment or launch an app. There is no gatekeeper to apply to.
No single point of failure
Thousands of independent machines agree on one history. Switch one off and nothing happens.
Rules you can read
The rules are open code, and changing them needs public agreement, not a board meeting.
The price
Everything is public, nothing can be quietly undone, and there is no customer support. Remember this card in act 5.
01 · WHY DECENTRALIZE
ACT 02 · BITCOIN → ETHEREUM
2008: Bitcoin, money without a bank
On 31 October 2008, in the middle of a global banking crisis, someone calling themselves Satoshi Nakamoto posted a nine-page paper to a cryptography mailing list.
It answered the double-spend problem without any trusted party: a shared ledger, copied on every node, extended block by block.
The first block, mined in January 2009, carries a newspaper headline: "Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks."
What Bitcoin proved
  • Digital scarcity is possible
  • Strangers can agree without identities
  • Incentives can secure a network
  • Code can hold real value

A hash is a fingerprint
Feed any data into a hash function and you get a short fingerprint. Change one character and the fingerprint changes completely.
So tampering is loud
Edit one payment in block 101 and its fingerprint changes, so block 102 no longer matches, and nor does any block after it.
02 · BITCOIN → ETHEREUM
Proof of Work: a lottery you enter with electricity
01
Collect
Pending payments wait in a shared pool
02
Bundle
A miner packs them into a candidate block
03
Race
Guess numbers until the block's hash starts with enough zeros
04
Broadcast
The winner shares it; anyone can check it instantly
05
Reward
New coins and fees go to the winner
Why it is secure
To rewrite history, an attacker must redo all that work, faster than every honest miner combined.
Why it is costly
Security is bought with electricity and specialised chips, and mining pools concentrate power. Remember this for act 3.
02 · BITCOIN → ETHEREUM
Live: this laptop is mining right now
A real SHA-256 race at a toy difficulty of three zeros. Real Bitcoin blocks need around nineteen.
02 · BITCOIN → ETHEREUM
A revolution with a tiny instruction set
Bitcoin's scripting language is deliberately limited: no loops and almost no memory. Perfect for one job, moving coins safely, and nearly useless for anything else.
By 2013, developers wanted lending, exchanges, voting and games, and each idea needed its own new blockchain built from scratch.
A 19-year-old asked: why not one chain that can run any program?
BITCOIN
A calculator: one job, done provably, forever
ETHEREUM
A computer: runs any program you can pay for
02 · BITCOIN → ETHEREUM
QUICK QUIZ · 2 OF 5
SHOUT YOUR ANSWER
Ethereum is a computer anyone in the world can use. What stops someone running an infinite loop and freezing it?
A
Nothing: it would freeze
B
The Ethereum Foundation switches it off
C
The program runs out of gas money and stops
D
Miners vote to delete the program
C
CORRECT
The program runs out of gas money and stops
Every instruction costs gas, paid in ETH. An endless loop simply burns through its budget and halts. It is an economic answer to a famous problem: you cannot always predict whether a program will ever stop.
02 · BITCOIN → ETHEREUM
2015: Ethereum, the world computer
The EVM
One shared virtual machine. Every node runs the same code and reaches the same result; that agreement is the product.
Two kinds of accounts
People, controlled by private keys, and contracts, controlled by code. Both can hold money and act.
Gas
Every instruction has a price paid in ETH. You pay for what you compute, so an endless loop simply runs out of money.
2013
Whitepaper
2014
Public crowdsale
JUL 2015
Launch ("Frontier"), on Proof of Work
02 · BITCOIN → ETHEREUM
Reading: ethereum.org/whitepaper
Smart contracts: vending machines for agreements
Insert a coin, get a snack, no shopkeeper needed. A smart contract applies that idea to any agreement: escrow, auctions, loans, insurance, certificates.
  • Deployed once: nobody, not even its author, can quietly change it
  • Runs exactly as written: a promise, and a threat
  • Holds its own money: a bug is not a crash, it is an open vault
Escrow.sol · Solidity
contract Escrow {   address buyer;   address seller;   function release() external {     require(msg.sender == buyer);     payable(seller).transfer(       address(this).balance);   } }
02 · BITCOIN → ETHEREUM
What happens when you press "Send"
01
Sign
Your wallet signs it with your private key
02
Broadcast
It waits in a public queue, the mempool
03
Order
A block builder picks it and sets its place
04
Propose
A validator adds the block to the chain
05
Execute
Every node runs it on the EVM and updates state
06
Finalize
After ~13 minutes it can never be undone
STEP 02 IS PUBLIC
Bots can see your trade before it lands, and jump ahead of it.
STEP 03 IS POWER
Whoever orders transactions decides who gets in, and in what order.
STEP 06 IS SLOW
Thirteen minutes to "final" is an eternity for payments.
02 · BITCOIN → ETHEREUM
Why Ethereum won: everything plugs into everything
Any contract can call any other contract, without asking permission. Each new app becomes a building block for the next: "money Legos".
STABLECOIN
A digital dollar issued as a token
LENDING POOL
Deposited to earn interest
EXCHANGE
Receipt used as collateral to trade
YOUR APP
Built on all three, in a weekend
DeFi
Lending, trading and savings as open code
NFTs
Provable ownership of digital things
DAOs
Organisations governed by member votes
Identity
Certificates and credentials anyone can verify
02 · BITCOIN → ETHEREUM
This is no longer a toy
$4 trillion
total crypto market value, crossed for the first time in 2025
$46 trillion
stablecoin transaction volume in 2025, much of it settled on Ethereum and its rollups
716 million
people own crypto, but only 40–70 million actually use it onchain
Why the gap?
It is still too complicated, too slow, and too easy to get robbed. Those are the open problems of acts 4 and 5.

03 · PROOF OF STAKE & THE MERGE
ACT 03 · PROOF OF STAKE & THE MERGE
From burning electricity to putting money at risk
Proof of Work
Proof of Stake
Who writes blocks
Miners with specialised hardware
Validators who lock up 32 ETH
Security comes from
Electricity spent on guessing
Money posted as collateral
If you cheat
You wasted your electricity
Your stake is destroyed ("slashed")
Energy use
Very high
~99.95% lower
New ETH issued
High, to pay for mining
About 90% lower
The intuition: instead of proving you burned resources, you prove you have something to lose.
03 · PROOF OF STAKE & THE MERGE
Figures: ethereum.org, The Merge
How Proof of Stake picks who writes the next block
01 · STAKE
Deposit 32 ETH to become a validator. The deposit is your bond.
02 · PROPOSE
Every 12-second slot, one validator is picked at random to propose a block.
03 · ATTEST
Committees of other validators vote that the block is valid.
04 · FINALIZE
Once two-thirds of all stake has voted over two epochs (~13 min), the block is final.
1 EPOCH = 32 SLOTS × 12 SECONDS = 6.4 MINUTES · one proposer per slot
Slashing
Sign two conflicting blocks or votes and part of your stake is destroyed, and you are thrown out.
Why final means final
Reverting a finalized block would need at least a third of all staked ETH to be slashed: billions destroyed on purpose.
03 · PROOF OF STAKE & THE MERGE
Watch Proof of Stake tick
A simulation at 30× speed: every square is a 12-second slot with one randomly chosen proposer.
03 · PROOF OF STAKE & THE MERGE
"Ethereum 2.0": a migration that took years
2014–2019
Research
Years of work on making stake-based consensus safe ("Casper").
1 DEC 2020
Beacon Chain
A separate Proof of Stake chain runs alongside. Staking only, no user transactions.
JAN 2022
"Eth2" renamed
It becomes the consensus layer; the old chain is the execution layer.
6 SEP 2022
Bellatrix
The Beacon Chain is upgraded, ready to take over.
15 SEP 2022
The Merge
Proof of Work is switched off. Proof of Stake takes over.
APR 2023
Shapella
Stakers can finally withdraw their ETH.
Why so slow? The network was live the entire time, holding billions of dollars of other people's money, with no maintenance window and no undo.
03 · PROOF OF STAKE & THE MERGE
Source: ethereum.org, The Merge
The Merge: swapping the engine in mid-flight
EXECUTION CHAIN · PROOF OF WORK · SINCE 2015
BEACON CHAIN · PROOF OF STAKE · SINCE 2020
15 SEP 2022 · THE MERGE
ETHEREUM TODAY: ONE CHAIN, TWO LAYERS
ethereum.org's analogy: Ethereum was a spaceship already in flight. Engineers built a new engine alongside it, tested it for nearly two years, then swapped it in without stopping the ship.
On the day, users noticed nothing. Every account, balance and contract carried over; the old chain kept running transactions, and the Beacon Chain took over deciding who adds blocks.
03 · PROOF OF STAKE & THE MERGE
Source: ethereum.org, The Merge
What the Merge changed, and what it didn't
Changed
  • Energy use fell by about 99.95%
  • New ETH issuance fell by about 90%
  • Security now comes from staked capital and slashing
  • Zero downtime: every balance and contract carried over
Did not change
  • Fees and speed: that work came later, through rollups
  • Withdrawals: stakers waited until April 2023
  • Everyone on board: some miners forked off to "EthereumPoW"
A new risk: much of the staked ETH now sits with a few large staking pools and exchanges. If too few operators control too much stake, they could censor or stall the chain.
03 · PROOF OF STAKE & THE MERGE
Source: ethereum.org, The Merge
After the Merge: an upgrade roughly every six months
WHEN
UPGRADE
WHAT IT DID
Apr 2023
Shapella
Staking withdrawals switched on
Mar 2024
Dencun
"Blobs": cheap data space that slashed rollup fees
May 2025
Pectra
Smarter accounts and staking improvements
Dec 2025
Fusaka
PeerDAS: nodes check data by sampling it, not downloading all of it
Q4 2026 target
Glamsterdam
ePBS and block-level access lists. Live on the Sepolia testnet since 6 Oct 2026; mainnet date not yet set
The strategy so far: keep the main chain (L1) for security and settlement, and push volume to rollups (L2s) that post their data back to it.

ACT 04 · OPEN PROBLEMS
The Strawmap: Ethereum's open draft to 2030
A "strawman roadmap" published at strawmap.org by the Ethereum Foundation's protocol team, maintained by its architecture group (Justin, Thomas, Toni and Vitalik).
  • Born as a discussion starter at an EF workshop in January 2026
  • Seven forks by 2029, about one every six months
  • Three layers: consensus, data, execution
  • Updated at least quarterly; feedback welcome
In its own words, it is not a prediction but a coordination tool. It even notes that AI-accelerated research could shorten the timeline.
Glams.
Hegotá
I*
J* …
CONS.
ePBS
DATA
EXEC.
BALs
A simplified sketch. Dark boxes are "headliners": one consensus and one execution headliner per fork (Glamsterdam: ePBS and BALs).
04 · OPEN PROBLEMS: THE STRAWMAP
Source: strawmap.org (EF Protocol), FAQ
Five north stars, five unsolved problems
Fast L1
Finality in seconds
Today: a block every 12 seconds, final after about 13 minutes.
Gigagas L1
~10,000 TPS on L1
1 billion gas per second, via zkEVMs and real-time proving.
Teragas L2
~10M TPS on L2s
1 gigabyte per second of rollup data, via data availability sampling.
Post-quantum L1
Safe for centuries
Cryptography that quantum computers cannot break, via hash-based schemes.
Private L1
Privacy by default
Privacy as a first-class citizen, via shielded transfers.
Next four slides: speed, scale, fairness, and quantum safety.
Privacy gets its own act: act 5.
04 · OPEN PROBLEMS: THE STRAWMAP
Source: strawmap.org, "five simple north stars"
PROBLEM 1 · SPEED
Why does "final" take 13 minutes?
Today
~13 min
Strawmap goal
seconds
Why it matters
Exchanges, payments and bridges between chains must wait for finality before they can safely treat money as received.
Why it is hard
Hundreds of thousands of validators must vote. Gathering and combining their signatures in seconds is a networking and cryptography problem.
The catch
Faster blocks favour big, well-connected operators. Speed must not cost decentralization.
04 · OPEN PROBLEMS: THE STRAWMAP
Sources: strawmap.org · Vitalik Buterin on fast finality (Sep 2026)
PROBLEM 2 · SCALE
Grow 200× without pushing anyone out
TODAY
New block arrives
Every node re-runs every transaction
Throughput capped by a modest PC
GOAL
New block arrives
One prover makes a ZK proof in real time
Every node checks the proof in milliseconds
The targets
L1: from about 5 million to 1 billion gas per second. L2: 1 gigabyte per second of data, checked by sampling.
Still unsolved
Can proofs be made fast and cheap enough? Will provers centralize? How do we stop stored state growing forever?
04 · OPEN PROBLEMS: THE STRAWMAP
Sources: strawmap.org · 4pillars, "Ethereum in 2030"
PROBLEM 3 · FAIRNESS
Who decides what gets into a block?
You
submit a token swap
Mempool
public: bots see it first
Builder
orders transactions for maximum profit
Relay
a trusted middleman passes the block on
Proposer
signs the most profitable block
MEV
Profit from ordering. A bot buys just before your trade and sells just after: a "sandwich". A few builders now make most blocks.
ePBS · Glamsterdam
Enshrined proposer-builder separation writes the builder–proposer deal into the protocol, removing the trusted relay.
FOCIL
Inclusion lists let many validators force transactions in, so a handful of builders cannot censor them.
04 · OPEN PROBLEMS: THE STRAWMAP
Sources: strawmap.org · Everstake, Strawmap explained
Watch a sandwich attack happen
A simulation with illustrative numbers. On a real chain the whole thing happens inside one block.
04 · OPEN PROBLEMS: THE STRAWMAP
PROBLEM 4 · QUANTUM SAFETY
A clock nobody can see
Every wallet and validator is protected by elliptic-curve signatures. A large enough quantum computer could work out private keys from public ones. Nobody knows when, and moving a live network takes years, so the work starts now.
TODAY
Elliptic-curve keys everywhere
STEP 1
Register post-quantum keys
STEP 2
Migrate wallets and validators
GOAL
Hash-based signatures only
The plan
Signatures whose security rests only on hash functions, rolled out over several forks.
The bet
The EF formed a post-quantum team in January 2026, with $1M in prizes for hash-function research.
Still hard
The new signatures are far bigger, and every user must move. What about lost or forgotten wallets?
04 · OPEN PROBLEMS: THE STRAWMAP
Sources: strawmap.org · 4pillars, "Ethereum in 2030"
ACT 05 · PRIVACY & SECURITY
Everything is public. Everything is final. Everything is a target.
The properties that make Ethereum trustworthy also make its failures unforgiving. Two questions for this act: who can see your money, and how does it get stolen?
05 · PRIVACY & SECURITY
PROBLEM 5 · PRIVACY
Today, every transaction is a postcard
TODAY · POSTCARD
from: 0x3a…91 to: 0x7f…c2 amount: 2.4 ETH · history: all of it
Anyone can read who paid whom, how much, and everything before it, forever.
GOAL · SEALED ENVELOPE
from: ████████ to: ████████ amount: ████ · valid: ✓ proven
A shielded transfer: the network checks it is valid without reading what is inside.
Why it matters
Public balances paint targets: thieves know exactly who holds what.
Being built
Privacy inside ordinary wallets; Privacy Pools prove funds are clean without revealing history.
The stakes
Without privacy, the EF's privacy team warns of "the backbone of global surveillance."
05 · PRIVACY & SECURITY
Sources: Vitalik, L1 privacy roadmap (Apr 2025) · PSE roadmap (Sep 2025)
The tool behind it all: zero-knowledge proofs
PROVER
Knows a secret: a balance, an identity, a model's weights
PROOF
A few hundred bytes, checkable in milliseconds
VERIFIER
Learns the statement is true, and nothing else
The Where's Waldo trick: cover the page with a big sheet that has one Waldo-sized hole. You prove you found him without revealing where he is on the page.
Privacy
Pay, vote or show a certificate without exposing yourself
Scaling
Prove a whole block was executed correctly (problem 2)
AI
Prove a model really produced an answer (act 6)
05 · PRIVACY & SECURITY
Idea: Goldwasser, Micali & Rackoff (1985)
How much money leaks out
$2.2B
$2.17B
$3.4B+
ALL OF 2024
H1 2025 ONLY
ALL OF 2025
One attack, most of the losses
Bybit's $1.5B was about 69% of everything stolen from services in the first half of 2025.
Nation-state attackers
North Korea-linked hackers took 61% of all stolen funds in 2024; the FBI tied Bybit to them too.
Individuals are targets now
Personal-wallet hacks and physical "wrench attacks" are rising.
05 · PRIVACY & SECURITY
Sources: Chainalysis 2025 mid-year update and annual estimates · FBI
Four ways the money leaves
Contract bugs
Logic errors, reentrancy, broken access checks. The DAO in 2016; Balancer, $121M, in 2025.
Keys and signing
Stolen keys and doctored signing screens. The biggest single losses now come from here.
People
Phishing, fake airdrops, look-alike addresses, rug pulls. The attacker only needs you to click once.
No privacy
Public balances and histories are free reconnaissance: attackers choose victims by reading the chain.
Almost never the blockchain itself. The protocol holds; the code and the people around it fail. In 2025, key theft caused the biggest losses, while contract exploits got smaller but more frequent.
05 · PRIVACY & SECURITY
Sources: Finbold 2025 report (SlowMist data) · Chainalysis

SHOUT YOUR ANSWER
In February 2025, attackers stole $1.5 billion from the exchange Bybit. What did they actually break?
A
Ethereum's cryptography
B

05 · PRIVACY & SECURITY
CASE STUDY · KEYS AND SIGNING
Bybit, February 2025: the screen lied
01 BREACH
Attackers break into a developer's machine at the wallet software provider
02 PLANT
They hide malicious code in the web page the signers use
03 DISGUISE
Bybit's signers see what looks like a routine transfer
04 SIGN
They approve it, really handing control of the cold wallet to the attacker
05 DRAIN
About 401,000 ETH, worth ~$1.5B, is moved out
No contract was broken
The multi-signature wallet did exactly what it was told. The humans were shown the wrong thing.
Open problem
What you see must be what you sign: readable, independently verified transaction displays.
Who
The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea's "TraderTraitor" group.
05 · PRIVACY & SECURITY
Sources: FBI attribution · post-incident reporting, Feb–Mar 2025
CASE STUDY · CODE
Why a contract bug is worse than a normal bug
Immutable
You cannot hot-fix what you cannot change.
Public
Every attacker can read it, copy it, and rehearse the attack in private.
Holds money
The exploit and the payout are the same transaction.
Composable
It inherits every flaw of every contract it calls.
"Move fast and break things" does not survive contact with a vault.
05 · PRIVACY & SECURITY
CHALLENGE · FIRST CORRECT ANSWER WINS
30 SECONDS
Spot the bug that could drain this contract
function withdraw() {   uint amount = balance[msg.sender];   require(amount > 0);   msg.sender.call{value: amount}("");   balance[msg.sender] = 0; }
HINT
Look at the order of the last two lines. What if whoever receives the money is itself a contract?
The bug: it sends the money before setting the balance to zero. If the receiver's code calls withdraw() again, the balance is still full, so it gets paid again, and again. This exact pattern drained The DAO in 2016.
05 · PRIVACY & SECURITY
The DAO, 2016: four lines that split Ethereum
01
Attacker calls withdraw()
02
The DAO sends the ETH before updating the balance
03
Receiving ETH runs attacker code that calls withdraw() again
04
The balance is set to zero only at the end. Too late.
↺ repeats until drained
function withdraw() {   uint amt = balance[msg.sender];   msg.sender.call{value: amt}(""); // send   balance[msg.sender] = 0;        // too late }
The fix: set the balance to zero before sending.
The DAO held about 14% of all ETH. Some 3.6M ETH was drained. The community hard-forked to return the funds; those who refused kept the old chain, today's Ethereum Classic.
05 · PRIVACY & SECURITY
The visibility problem: most contracts can't be read
<5%
of roughly 60 million deployed Ethereum contracts have published source code
WHAT DEVS WRITE
function withdraw() { … }
Readable, auditable
WHAT THE CHAIN STORES
0x608060405234 8015600f57…
Bytecode, no names, often obfuscated
Decompile
Turn bytecode back into something a human or a tool can audit.
See through obfuscation
Scammers deliberately scramble code. Can we detect it, or undo it?
Analyse at scale
Millions of contracts, too many for humans. This is where AI comes in.
05 · PRIVACY & SECURITY
ACT 06 · AI × CRYPTO
AI centralizes. Crypto decentralizes.
AI today
  • A few labs control the frontier models and the compute
  • You cannot check which model answered you, or what trained it
  • Fake people and fake content are almost free to make
  • AI agents cannot open bank accounts
What blockchains add
  • Open, permissionless access that no one can revoke
  • Verifiable computation and public, tamper-evident records
  • Proof that a person, or an agent, is unique
  • Money that software can hold and spend
AI is getting more powerful and more concentrated. Blockchains are good at exactly the trust problems that creates.
06 · AI × CRYPTO
Framing: a16z crypto, "AI x crypto: what, where, how"
Four roles AI can play in crypto
AI as a player
Agents act inside crypto systems: trading, arbitrage, prediction markets. Already happening.
AI as the interface
AI explains what you are about to sign and flags scams. Recall Bybit: the screen lied.
AI as the rules
A contract that obeys an AI judge. Riskiest: attackers can study the model and craft inputs that fool it.
AI as the objective
Use crypto to build better AI: shared compute, open data markets, decentralized training.
06 · AI × CRYPTO
After Vitalik Buterin, "The promise and challenges of crypto + AI applications" (2024)
Four trust problems AI has, four tools crypto offers
THE AI PROBLEM
THE CRYPTO TOOL
Who is real? Deepfakes, bots and fake accounts
Proof of personhood Prove you are a unique human, privately
How does an agent pay? Software cannot open a bank account
Wallets and agent standards ERC-8004 for identity, x402 for payments
Which model answered? You cannot check what actually ran
Verifiable inference Zero-knowledge proofs of the computation
Can I trust the model at all? Poisoned data, swapped weights
Public provenance records A tamper-evident log of data, training and models
06 · AI × CRYPTO
Source: a16z crypto, "AI needs crypto, especially now" (Feb 2026)
Who is real? Proof of personhood
With deepfakes, bots and impersonation nearly free, we need a way to know we are dealing with a real, unique person. a16z calls uniqueness, being unable to fake a second identity, non-negotiable.
01 · VERIFY ONCE
Prove you are a unique human, once
02 · HOLD IT
A credential sits in your own wallet
03 · PROVE IT
Show an app a ZK proof: "real, and new here"
04 · NOTHING ELSE
The app never learns who you are
Why a blockchain
No single company owns your identity, and it works across every app.
An example
World ID uses iris scans so that a second identity is nearly impossible.
Still open
Biometric privacy, people left out, and who runs the verifiers.
06 · AI × CRYPTO
Sources: a16z crypto, Big Ideas 2025 · "AI needs crypto" (2026)
QUICK QUIZ · 5 OF 5
SHOUT YOUR ANSWER
AI agents are reviving an HTTP status code that sat unused for nearly 30 years. Which one?
A
404 Not Found
B
402 Payment Required
C
418 I'm a teapot
D
451 Unavailable For Legal Reasons
B
CORRECT
402 Payment Required
HTTP 402 was reserved "for future use" in the 1990s. The x402 protocol finally uses it: a server replies 402 with a price, the agent pays in stablecoins, and gets the data. (418 is real too: a 1998 April Fools' joke.)
06 · AI × CRYPTO
Agents that find, trust and pay each other
01 NEED
An AI agent needs a dataset to finish its task
02 DISCOVER
Finds providers in the ERC-8004 identity registry
03 CHECK
Reads their reputation, recorded onchain
04 PAY
Server replies "402: Payment Required"; the agent pays cents in stablecoins
05 REVIEW
Gets the data and leaves feedback onchain
ERC-8004
Live on Ethereum since late January 2026: registries for identity, reputation and validation. 49,000+ agents registered by mid-February.
x402
Revives the web's unused HTTP 402 code for pay-per-request. Google has worked with Coinbase on agent payments.
Still open
Fake agents gaming reputation, and agents tricked by prompt injection into signing bad transactions.
06 · AI × CRYPTO
Sources: Cointelegraph (Feb 2026) · Chainstack, ERC-8004 explainer
Which model answered? Verifiable inference
01 COMMIT
Publish a fingerprint of the model's weights onchain
02 RUN
Run the model off-chain on the input
03 PROVE
ZK proof: this model, on this input, gave this output
04 VERIFY
A smart contract checks the proof in milliseconds
05 ACT
Pay out, settle a market, approve a loan
The input and the weights can stay private: anyone can check the answer is honest without seeing either.
Uses
AI oracles, prediction-market resolution, credit scoring, medical models on private data.
Reality check
Proving is still far slower and costlier than running the model. Big language models are out of reach today.
The shortcut
Secure hardware enclaves attest which code ran: fast, but you trust the chip maker.
06 · AI × CRYPTO
Tools to explore: EZKL · Lagrange DeepProve · JSTprove (arXiv 2025)
Securing the ML pipeline with a public ledger
Data
Risk: poisoned or unlicensed data
Record: dataset hashes and licences
Training
Risk: silent changes to the recipe
Record: config and checkpoints, committed
Model
Risk: swapped or tampered weights
Record: a signed weight fingerprint
Serving
Risk: a cheaper model served instead
Record: a proof or attestation per answer
Output
Risk: untraceable fakes
Record: signed provenance for content
What the ledger adds
Timestamps nobody can backdate, records no single company can edit, and checks anyone can rerun.
The honest caveat
A blockchain proves what was recorded and when, not that it was true. It is an audit trail, not a truth machine.
06 · AI × CRYPTO
The twist: AI is already breaking smart contracts
SHARE OF RECENTLY HACKED CONTRACTS AI AGENTS COULD EXPLOIT
A year earlier
2%
Late 2025
55.8%
Simulated exploit revenue on these contracts rose from about $5,000 to $4.6 million, roughly doubling every 1.3 months.
The study
SCONE-bench: 405 contracts really exploited in 2020–2025, attacked in simulation by frontier AI agents.
New bugs, not just old ones
Scanning 2,849 live contracts with no known flaws, agents found two brand-new vulnerabilities.
So defenders need AI too
AI auditors, AI-assisted formal verification, and tools that read the 95% of contracts nobody can.
06 · AI × CRYPTO
Source: Anthropic & MATS, SCONE-bench study (Dec 2025)
